1. Background and rationale
People living with HIV (PLWH) may benefit from solid-organ transplantation, but HIV-related transplant experience varies across centers. The HIV Organ Policy Equity (HOPE) Act created a pathway for transplantation from donors with HIV to recipients with HIV. Regulatory requirements differ by organ and calendar period, and geographic proximity to a center does not establish clinical eligibility or program willingness to accept a candidate.
This study describes the geographic distribution of access to adult solid-organ transplant centers among PLWH and people without HIV, and distinguishes access to any active center from access to centers with documented HIV recipient or HIV-positive donor experience.

2. Objectives

2.1 Co-primary descriptive objectives
The primary geographic reach measure is a 60-minute driving isochrone. Each objective is evaluated separately for kidney, liver, heart, lung and pancreas, in 2017 and 2022.

P1 — Access by HIV status: Estimate the percentage of PLWH and the percentage of people without HIV residing within the catchment of any active adult transplant center, and their difference in percentage points (PLWH minus people without HIV).
P2 — Access by center experience: Among PLWH, estimate the percentages residing within reach of (a) any active adult center, (b) an active HIV R+ center and (c) an active HOPE D+ center, and the percentage-point differences between these categories.



2.2 Secondary objectives

S1 — Alternative reach distances: Repeat P1 and P2 with 50-, 100- and 200-mile straight-line catchments.
S2 — Temporal comparison: Describe 2017-to-2022 differences in each estimate in percentage points, not relative percentage change. The two years are snapshots, not a longitudinal trend series.
S3 — Population stratification: Estimate geographic coverage by race/ethnicity, sex, age group and geographic region where comparable HIV surveillance counts and corresponding population denominators support meaningful estimates. Document unavailable or suppressed strata rather than treating missing values as zero. Stratified comparisons are descriptive and conditional on data feasibility and quality.
S4 — Potential center expansion: Among active centers without documented HIV R+ transplantation in the relevant five-year window, estimate the incremental number and percentage of PLWH who would lie within reach if a candidate center began offering HIV transplant services. Identify high-yield candidates by additional population covered beyond the existing HIV R+ network, accounting for overlap. This models hypothetical expansion of service availability, not actual feasibility or uptake.



2.3 Exploratory objective
Describe the estimated number of PLWH within individual active centers’ catchments according to center experience category: HOPE D+, HIV R+ without HOPE D+ experience, and no documented HIV R+ experience. This is descriptive, not inferential.

3. Study design and setting
Repeated cross-sectional, ecological geospatial analysis of the 48 contiguous states and Washington, DC. Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and other territories are outside the study geography for both population and center analyses.
The index years are 2017 and 2022. Historical center experience is defined within five calendar years ending in each index year (2013–2017 and 2018–2022). Population estimates correspond to each index year. Geographic coverage is attributed to residential areas, not to individual patients or observed transplant referrals. SRTR patient-level records are used only to classify centers and derive experience measures; there is no patient-level linkage to community HIV surveillance data.

4. Data sources and measurement periods







Source
Time basis and intended contribution




SRTR transplant and relevant donor records
Historical activity and transplant experience for each organ and five-year window; restricted patient-level source


Historical transplant-center records, including HRSA/OPTN or comparable authoritative sources
Center identity, organ service and location at the applicable index year; historical reconstruction is required


CDC NCHHSTP AtlasPlus HIV prevalence
County counts of diagnosed PLWH corresponding to each index year; verify age coverage and compatible state totals


American Community Survey 5-year estimates
County and tract populations for 2017 and 2022; age 13+ for the primary analysis, and all ages for a sensitivity analysis


Mapbox or comparably specified road-routing source
Modeled 60-minute driving catchments using a common contemporary road-network methodology for both historical snapshots


Census geographic boundaries
Appropriate county/tract geographic vintages; changes in geographic definitions, including Connecticut, require reconciliation



The primary analysis requires index-year center locations, but does not require a historical road-network reconstruction. Contemporary road-network and traffic assumptions applied consistently to the two years should be disclosed as a modeling limitation. Source vintages and retrieval assumptions must be sufficiently documented to interpret the findings.

5. Study populations and transplant-center definitions

5.1 Transplant-center cohorts
Definitions apply separately by organ and index year. All three analytic center categories are nested:

Active: A geographically eligible program with at least one qualifying adult transplant of that organ in the index calendar year (adult defined as age 18+ at transplant).
HIV R+: An active center with at least one qualifying adult recipient living with HIV transplanted in the five-year window ending in the index year.
HOPE D+: An active HIV R+ center with at least one qualifying adult HIV D+/R+ transplant using a deceased donor with HIV in the same five-year window.

Thus, HOPE D+ ⊆ HIV R+ ⊆ active. HIV-positive living-donor transplants are not included in the HOPE D+ classification. Because such donations are uncommon, omission is expected to have little impact on center classification, but the extent of any difference can be checked if reliably identifiable data are available. Confirm as a simple validation check whether restricting HOPE D+ centers to index-year-active programs excludes any programs; do not treat a null difference as a standalone sensitivity analysis.
Organ definitions: Kidney activity and experience include qualifying kidney-alone and simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplants. Pancreas activity and experience include qualifying pancreas-alone and simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplants. A simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplant may contribute to both organ-specific analyses, but must not appear twice within either organ-specific count. Determine the handling of other combined-organ procedures consistently with the source definitions and avoid double counting. Actual SRTR file contents and transplant-type coding must be verified during implementation.
Center HIV experience is a proxy for past experience, not a demonstration of current willingness, clinical capacity, or candidacy acceptance.


5.2 Geographic population groups

PLWH: County prevalence counts of diagnosed HIV obtained from AtlasPlus, allocated to census tracts proportionally to their resident population aged 13+.
People without HIV: ACS resident population aged 13+ minus the estimated tract PLWH count.

This primary age alignment is conditional on verifying that the selected AtlasPlus HIV prevalence indicator covers ages 13+. It is a population-measure alignment, not an assertion that adolescents are eligible for adult transplant programs. Adults and pediatric patients use different transplant systems; the population aged 13–17 is retained because reliably age-disaggregated county HIV counts may not support an 18+ estimate. The effect of using all-age ACS population is examined separately.

6. Population estimation and suppressed counts

6.1 County-to-tract allocation
For county c and tract t within that county:
[ {t}=H{c}, ]
where (H_c) is the county diagnosed-PLWH count and (P_{13+}) is resident population aged 13+. The county and tract age denominators should refer to compatible geographic units and periods. Population-proportional allocation is an ecological estimate assuming uniform HIV prevalence within each county; the resulting tract counts are not measured tract-level HIV counts. Totals must reconcile at the county level within rounding. Zero-denominator and missing county cases require explicit handling.


6.2 Suppressed county estimates
The planned method will be implemented in the {CDCAtlas} package, not independently recreated in the analysis repository. Within each state, subtract the sum of reported nonsuppressed county HIV counts from the comparable state total; allocate the nonnegative residual among suppressed counties in proportion to their relevant populations. Preserve the original observed-versus-imputed status and reconcile the completed county totals to state totals, allowing for published rounding. If state and county totals differ in scope, age definition, geography or vintage—or the residual is inconsistent—the discrepancy must be resolved or reported before applying this method.
This is an agreed planned method, not a claim that {CDCAtlas} already implements it. An alternative zero-fill treatment of suppressed counties is a prespecified sensitivity analysis.

7. Historical center linkage and geography
Historical location reconstruction for both index years is required. SRTR supplies activity and center identifiers; index-year location and program identity should be established using historical authoritative records rather than automatically carrying back current coordinates. Differences due to relocation, opening, closing, or identifier changes matter insofar as they affect geographically modeled coverage.
Linkage quality should be checked in proportion to its analytic impact: summarize numbers matched and unmatched, flag ambiguous or materially consequential unresolved centers, and investigate those cases as needed. There is no requirement for manual verification of every automatically matched center, or for a published linkage-audit table. Do not silently interpret a missing historical center location as evidence that the center did not exist.
County-to-ACS joins, county-to-tract assignments and any altered county-equivalent geography (notably Connecticut) must be reconciled sufficiently to avoid loss or duplication of HIV counts. Different tract boundary vintages do not imply that individual tract observations can be directly compared across years; cross-year comparisons focus on aggregate coverage.

8. Geographic reach and outcomes

8.1 Catchments

Primary: 60-minute modeled driving isochrone for each center, at 7:00 AM local time on a weekday, with consistent routing assumptions across the 2017 and 2022 comparisons. The previously selected reference weekdays were March 6, 2017 and March 7, 2022; these are reference departure conventions, not evidence of historical traffic conditions.
Secondary: 50-, 100- and 200-mile straight-line buffers, computed in an appropriate projected coordinate system with distance units converted consistently.

For any organ, year, reach measure and center category, combine center catchments into a union before estimating population coverage so that overlapping catchments do not double-count residents.


8.2 Primary tract inclusion rule and denominator
A tract is considered covered if any part of its geometry intersects the union of eligible center catchments. All of its estimated PLWH or non-HIV population then contributes to the numerator. The denominator is the corresponding estimated population over the entire study geography in that year. Coverage is reported as a percentage to one decimal place, with contrasts in percentage points. Any-intersection can overstate access, particularly in large rural tracts; a geometric centroid rule is a prespecified sensitivity analysis.
Non-HIV geographic coverage is evaluated for the active center group (P1). PLWH coverage is evaluated for all three nested groups (P2).
When a group has no qualifying centers, report 0% with a clear “no qualifying centers” label. When qualifying centers exist but the modeled population covered is zero, report 0% without that label. Missing or unresolved input data yield undetermined, not zero. Report qualifying center counts alongside coverage findings.

9. Analysis and interpretation

9.1 Stratified geographic access (S3)
For each feasible subgroup and organ/year, use appropriately matched subgroup HIV counts and population denominators to estimate coverage under the same catchment and tract-inclusion definitions as the main study. Evaluate suppression, geographic completeness and reconciliation before interpreting subgroup differences. Where fine-grained age bands or intersections of demographic characteristics cannot be estimated reliably, report the limitation and omit unsupported strata rather than fabricate precision. Geographic regions must be defined consistently for the comparison. Subgroup analyses are descriptive and should not be interpreted as individual-level disparities in transplant referral or receipt.


9.2 Potential expansion of HIV R+ services (S4)
Take the union of catchments for active HIV R+ centers as the existing service network. For each eligible active non-HIV R+ center, calculate the additional estimated PLWH covered by its catchment outside that existing union, using the same index-year population and reach definition. Report absolute newly covered PLWH and change in coverage in percentage points; a candidate’s total catchment population is not its marginal gain. Individual candidate gains are not additive when candidate catchments overlap. If illustrating a sequence of multiple additions, recalculate marginal gain after each hypothetical addition instead of summing standalone gains. This is a geographic prioritization scenario, not evidence that a center will or can initiate an HIV transplant program. Center ranking is descriptive and does not equate geographic benefit with clinical readiness.


9.3 Interpretation and inference
The co-primary and secondary estimates are descriptive population quantities. Report the percentages and prespecified percentage-point contrasts; do not calculate confidence intervals, conduct hypothesis tests or report relative percentage changes. The major uncertainties concern spatial allocation, suppressed counts, center location and routing assumptions, rather than sampling variation. Prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluate selected structural assumptions, but do not exhaust all sources of uncertainty.
For the exploratory per-center comparison, estimate PLWH within each individual center’s catchment and display distributions, medians and appropriate descriptive plots across mutually exclusive experience categories. Individual center catchments overlap and may share tracts; centers can also appear in both years. Do not perform Kruskal–Wallis or other hypothesis tests for these comparisons, and do not infer a causal effect of local HIV population on center experience or vice versa.

10. Missing data and validity requirements

Distinguish missing, unknown or not-done HIV status from demonstrated positive status when classifying recipients and donors. Document the handling of such records.
Do not silently equate a suppressed county HIV count with zero in the primary analysis; retain observed/imputed indicators and reconcile sums.
Verify that county-level HIV counts allocated to tracts reconcile with their parent counties and that estimated PLWH plus people without HIV reconcile with the corresponding ACS population base.
Check matching and inclusion of historical centers and identify unresolved records with material potential impact; confirm nested center-group counts and membership.
Confirm eligible-center catchments, valid geometries, uniform geography exclusions and absence of double counting in catchment unions or organ-specific transplant counts.
Verify logically ordered results: 50-mile coverage must not exceed 100-mile coverage, which must not exceed 200-mile coverage; HOPE D+ coverage must not exceed HIV R+, which must not exceed active coverage, for a shared organ, year and reach measure.
Explicitly distinguish empty center groups, uncovered populations and data failures.
For subgroup coverage, reconcile source totals and denominators where comparable, track suppression and geographic completeness, and identify strata that cannot support estimation.
For center expansion, verify that candidates are active and not already HIV R+ centers, and that newly covered tracts are not already in the existing catchment; avoid summing overlapping candidate gains.

These checks are internal analytic requirements. They do not mandate a published validation appendix or manual line-by-line audit. Material unresolved discrepancies should be corrected or disclosed before results are treated as final.

11. Prespecified sensitivity analyses
All three analyses will be performed and documented. Material changes in interpretation should be included in the manuscript; results may otherwise appear in supplementary materials rather than the main text.







Analysis
Alternative to primary method




SA-suppression
Fill suppressed county HIV counts with zero rather than state-residual, population-proportional estimates


SA-tract
Count a tract only if its geometric centroid lies within the unioned catchment, rather than using any-intersection


SA-age
Use all-age ACS population for geographic allocation and the non-HIV population comparison rather than an age-13+ base, consistent with the original analysis



The 50-, 100- and 200-mile buffer analyses are secondary objectives, not additional sensitivity analyses. No separate sensitivity analysis is required for historical road networks, alternative departure times, alternative county-to-tract allocation, or unrestricted HOPE D+ centers, apart from the checks already described.

12. Limitations

Ecological estimation: HIV counts are observed at county level and allocated to tracts under uniform within-county prevalence; within-county clustering and partial-tract coverage are not directly measured.
Diagnosed HIV only: Undiagnosed HIV is not counted in the source HIV surveillance measure.
Geographic potential rather than realized access: Proximity does not establish clinical need, referral, ability to travel, insurance coverage, program acceptance, or receipt of transplant.
Age/clinical-system mismatch: The 13+ population measure includes adolescents, whereas center activity is defined by adult transplantation; adolescent HIV burden is expected to be small but is not necessarily separately identifiable in county data.
Center experience as proxy: Previous HIV R+ or deceased-donor HIV D+/R+ transplantation need not indicate contemporary willingness or capacity; living-donor HIV D+/R+ experience is not separately classified.
Historical and contemporary measurement: Historical center locations and populations are combined with contemporary road-network and traffic assumptions; estimates do not recover historical driving conditions.
Geographic and time limitations: Contiguous US and DC only; two cross-sectional years; changes in tract boundaries and county equivalents complicate small-area comparisons.
Source data quality: HIV classification, center linkage, suppression and revisions to surveillance or geographic data may alter results.
Subgroup coverage: Differential suppression, incompatible denominator categories and incomplete demographic stratification may limit comparisons across population groups.
Expansion scenarios: Marginal geographic coverage does not establish a center’s clinical readiness, willingness, staffing, referral patterns or patients’ realized access.

13. Required scientific results
The analysis must produce, for each organ and index year: counts of centers by nested experience group; relevant population totals; 60-minute geographic coverage estimates for both co-primary objectives; prespecified percentage-point contrasts; secondary distance-buffer coverage; 2017-to-2022 percentage-point differences; descriptive center-level catchment population comparisons; feasible, quality-assessed population subgroup comparisons; and a descriptive ranking of potential HIV R+ center expansion by incremental geographic coverage. Prespecified sensitivity analyses must be documented, with material effects reported.
Maps, tables, figures and manuscript ordering are presentation choices and are not fixed by this analysis plan.

14. Reproducibility and data access
The study relies on restricted SRTR records and publicly available population, surveillance and geographic sources, as well as modeled routing data. Restricted, patient-level SRTR information must not be published or transferred into public analysis outputs. The analysis should be reproducible within an authorized environment from defined data vintages and methodological assumptions. Repository-specific execution, version-recording, cache management and contributor instructions belong in AGENTS.md; the current implementation and data flow belong in ARCHITECTURE.md. Extensions using longer driving times or transit, and Bayesian county-to-tract modeling, are potential subsequent studies rather than requirements of this plan.

title: Unite buffers
text:
This script combines individual transplant center buffers into unified, organ-level catchment areas.
Earlier steps created buffers (either distance-based or 60-minute travel-time isochrones) around each transplant center.
Here, those individual polygons are merged into a single combined service area for each organ, distance, and year.

title: Unite buffers
text:
Why “Unite” Buffers?
When buffers are created around multiple centers, they often:

Overlap geographically

Cover adjacent regions

Share common areas

If we simply summed tract populations within each individual buffer, overlapping areas would be double-counted.
To prevent this, we:

Combine (union) all individual center buffers
Create a single, continuous polygon representing the total catchment area
Ensure that each geographic area is counted only once

title: Unite buffers
text:

Four parallel objects are constructed:

Transplant_center_all_buffer_united
Transplant_centers_active_buffer_united
Transplant_centers_HIV_buffer_united
Transplant_centers_HOPE_buffer_united

Each object is indexed by:

Organ

title: Unite buffers
text:
How the Union Works
For each:

Organ
Distance
(And year, when relevant)

The script:

Takes the set of individual buffer polygons
Applies st_union(geometry)

Collapses them into one merged geometry
Converts the result back into an {sf} object

The resulting dataset contains a single row labeled:
catchment_area = “All Centers”
This label clarifies that the polygon represents the combined service area of all centers in that category.

title: Unite buffers
text:
Structure of the Result
After processing, the structure is:

Transplant_center_all_buffer_united[[organ]][[distance]]
Transplant_centers_active_buffer_united[[organ]][[distance]][[year]]
Transplant_centers_HIV_buffer_united[[organ]][[distance]][[year]]
Transplant_centers_HOPE_buffer_united[[organ]][[distance]][[year]]

Each object is a single merged polygon representing the total geographic coverage of that center group.

title: Unite buffers
text:
Why This Step Matters
Uniting buffers allows accurate calculation of:

Total population within service areas
Total number of people living with HIV within reach
Changes in geographic access between years
Comparisons across center categories (Active vs HIV vs HOPE)

Without uniting overlapping buffers, population totals would be inflated and geographic access overstated.

title: Classify centers

Initialize lists
This portion of the code initializes lists to classify transplant centers by activity status and HIV transplant volume for each organ and year of interest. These classifications are used downstream for geographic access analyses, state-level summaries, and figure generation.
For example, the nested list HOPE_center_volumes can be used to identify the number of HIV D+/R+ transplants performed at each transplant center for each organ and each time period.
HOPE_center_volumes[["kidney"]][["2017"]] will yield a data frame of HOPE kidney volumes for centers that performed at least one HOPE adult transplant in the 2013-2017 time period.
Key lists created:

Active_tx_centers: any adult transplant in the year defined by the inner list
HIV_center_volumes: any HIV R+ transplant in the five-year period
HOPE_center_volumes: any HIV D+/R+ transplant in the five-year period
State_level_transplant_volumes: HIV R+ volumes by state
Transplant_centers_active: similar to the first list active_tx_centers but with different variable composition

      mutate(year_transplant=year(REC_TX_DT))%>%
      filter(year_transplant==as.numeric(year_loop))%>%

      filter(REC_HIV_STAT=="P")%>%
      filter(REC_AGE_IN_MONTHS_AT_TX>=216)%>% #Adult recipient

      group_by(REC_CTR_CD)%>%

      mutate(year_transplant=year(REC_TX_DT ))%>%

      filter(OTCCode %in% Active_tx_centers[[organ_loop]][[year_loop]])

title: Set isochrones
text:
The code in this script creates 60-minute driving catchment areas around transplant centers.
These catchment areas are later used to estimate how many people living with HIV reside within a realistic travel time of transplant programs.

title: Set isochrones
text:
Creating 60-Minute Driving Catchment Areas
This section generates travel-time–based service areas for transplant centers.
Unlike simple radius buffers (e.g., 50 miles in every direction), these service areas reflect actual road travel time, accounting for highways, traffic patterns, and geography.

What is an Isochrone?
An isochrone is a geographic area showing how far someone can travel within a specified amount of time.
In this analysis:

A 60-minute isochrone represents all locations that can be reached within 60 minutes of driving from a transplant center.
This provides a more realistic measure of geographic access than straight-line (circular) buffers.

Isochrones are generated using the {mapboxapi} R package, which interfaces with the Mapbox routing API:

https://walker-data.com/mapboxapi/
CRAN: https://cran.r-project.org/package=mapboxapi

title: Set isochrones
text:
Standardizing Time: Why 7:00 AM?
Travel time varies depending on traffic conditions.
To ensure consistency:

Isochrones are calculated assuming departure at 7:00 AM local time.
This approximates peak commuting conditions.
Using a fixed time improves comparability across regions.

Because Mapbox requires time in UTC, the script:

Creates a 7:00 AM timestamp for each U.S. time zone
Converts that time to UTC using with_tz()
Stores these converted times in converted_times

This ensures that each transplant center’s isochrone is calculated at the correct local time.

title: Set isochrones
text:
Caching Isochrone Results
Generating isochrones requires external API calls and can be computationally expensive.
To avoid recomputing them repeatedly:

The script checks whether a cached .RDS file already exists.
If it exists → it loads the file.
If not → it generates the isochrone and saves it to the cache/ directory.

This dramatically speeds up Quarto re-rendering and ensures reproducibility.

The project
This is an R analysis project, not an R package. It estimates the share of people living with HIV (PLWH), and of people without HIV, who live within reach of an adult solid-organ transplant center in the contiguous United States, by organ, index year (2017 and 2022), center experience with HIV (active, HIV R+, HOPE D+) and reach definition (a 60-minute driving isochrone and 50-, 100- and 200-mile buffers). It combines SRTR transplant records, HRSA center locations, CDC AtlasPlus county HIV prevalence, ACS population counts and Mapbox isochrones. The code and methods are published as a Quarto website.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions in every area are made by Vagish Hemmige. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Do not make unresolved scientific decisions implicitly through code. Check the relevant open issues before implementing an analysis that depends on them.
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or {pkgdown} infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it. Do not impose the current global-object design on experiments.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a distance, a reference date) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects. Some existing helpers read globals (see ARCHITECTURE.md); new code does not add more.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute or Windows-specific paths, or writes outside the project. Restricted data are located only through their access package’s configuration.

Mark only what an open decision could change, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. _quarto.yml sets execute: eval: false. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the setup page’s package and constants tables, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, and the results pages, which read only site-outputs/, set eval: true.
Publishing. The site renders to docs/, which is not committed; .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check, and on every push to master renders and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/, which are gitignored because they derive from restricted SRTR data: agents may not open them (see Restricted data).
site-outputs/ holds the tables and figures the website shows. R/tables.R and the export-site-figures section of R/figures.R write it, and it is committed. Commit changes to it only after the disclosure check below; agents may read what is committed there. images/ holds the site’s images that no script makes.
cache/ holds Census pulls, isochrones and other intermediates and is gitignored. Caches are not invalidated automatically when upstream code, definitions, source data or routing assumptions change: identify stale dependencies and say what needs rebuilding, and do not assume a cached or published result is current. Ask before deleting caches.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers, person-level dates, or small geographies. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/, figures/ and cache/). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. Aggregates derived from SRTR data need review under the SRTR data use agreement before release, even though they are aggregated or cached. Take particular care with small cells and with center-specific information on HIV R+ and HOPE D+ transplantation, including the center-group outlines and beeswarm plots, and with counts recoverable by subtraction or complementary cells. Follow the agreement’s exact dissemination rules. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including site-outputs/, scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls, notably uncached Mapbox isochrones. Before a paid batch, make one call with the exact package version and settings, and check the result before running the rest. Which service or version to use is the person’s choice; an agent proposes, with the cost if known, and does not switch it on its own.

Public ACS, CDC AtlasPlus, HRSA, and Census data can be used subject to their own terms.

Coding conventions

Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every join of records to centers and every spatial join, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows. Keep FIPS codes and GEOIDs as zero-padded character strings.
Windows (the five-year experience windows and index years) are written as constants matching the plan, and their edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns spatial results into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Never invent variables, codes, files, or definitions; check SRTR variables and code values against the SRTR documentation for the release used.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory. A test that fakes a package checks only our own logic, so call the real package once (synthetic data, or one cheap call) before relying on the code.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when(), loops over names or named lists rather than the apply family, Reduce or positional indexing. Required base R goes in a named, tested function. Tidyverse layout; style changes in their own commits, and no unrelated stylistic rewrites during scientific changes.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use the access package’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing, suppressed, and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s definition, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code?
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, including site-outputs/, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from restricted data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?

Checks specific to this design:

Population: observed, suppressed, missing and estimated counts kept distinct; denominators and age strata compatible; county-to-tract allocation reconciles to county totals; missing or suppressed never silently equated with zero.
Centers: organ-specific activity, the classification windows, recipient and donor HIV definitions, historical location assumptions, and eligibility in each index year; no duplicate events within an organ.
Space: CRS and units (buffers are computed in EPSG:5070, in meters); geometry validity; the tract inclusion rule; geographic exclusions. Dissolved catchments for aggregate coverage; per-center catchments only where overlap is intended.
Travel time: driving isochrones, straight-line buffers, transit access and travel-time matrices kept conceptually separate; routing profile, reference times, coverage, API limits and cached results checked.
Results: an empty center group distinguished from missing inputs; denominators and plausibility checked; subgroups not assumed to nest unless the plan’s definitions require it.

Checks test scientific consequences and edge cases, not merely repeat the same calculation. Record which checks ran, which did not, and any data or credentials that were unavailable.

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline, deleting caches or making expensive calls; shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib, alongside the decisions they support.

title: Load data
section: Load US state maps from census
text:
Load US state maps from census
We import U.S. state boundary shapefiles using the {tigris} package.
The tigris::states() function retrieves state-level shapefiles from the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line products.

Column Selection
We retain only:

NAME → full state name
STUSPS → two-letter state abbreviation
geometry → polygon boundaries

This reduces memory overhead and keeps the object lightweight for downstream joins and plotting.


Exclusions
We remove:

Alaska and Hawaii (to avoid projection distortion in contiguous U.S. maps)
U.S. territories (not included in SRTR transplant center analyses)

This ensures that visualizations align with the contiguous U.S. study population.


Output
The resulting object, states_sf, is an {sf} object containing polygon geometries for the 48 contiguous U.S. states,

# Load US state maps from census
states_sf <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE, year = 2022)%>%
  select(NAME, STUSPS, geometry) %>%
  filter(!(NAME %in% c("Alaska", 
                       "Hawaii", 
                       "Puerto Rico", 
                       "United States Virgin Islands",
                       "Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands",
                       "Guam",
                       "American Samoa"))) %>%
  rename(State=NAME)

Load transplant center data from SRTR package
To map transplant center locations and define geographic catchment areas, we retrieve center-level data from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) using the {sRtr} package.
The get_hrsa_transplant_centers() function accesses HRSA transplant center metadata, including center identifiers and geographic coordinates.
Subsequent steps:

Remove Hawaii and Puerto Rico
Keep the following variables:

OTC_NM: transplant center name
OTC_CD: transplant center 4-letter UNOS code
Service_Lst: list of organs transplanted at that center
X, Y: longitude and latitude of transplant center

Keep transplant centers whose organ corresponds with the organ defined in the organ_loop variable for each loop
Removes duplicates with the distinct() command
Renames variables for convenience
Pauses for five seconds between iterations to avoid overloading the HRSA website



Click to show/hide R Code
# Load transplant center data from SRTR package
Transplant_centers_all<-list()

for (organ_loop in organ_list)
{
  
  
  Transplant_centers_all[[organ_loop]]<-sRtr::get_hrsa_transplant_centers()%>%
    filter(OPO_STATE_ABBR != "PR" & OPO_STATE_ABBR!= "HI")%>%
    select(OTC_NM, OTC_CD, Service_Lst, X, Y) %>%
    filter(str_detect(Service_Lst, str_to_sentence(organ_loop)))%>%
    select(-Service_Lst)%>%
    distinct()%>%
    rename(OTCName=OTC_NM, OTCCode=OTC_CD, Latitude=Y, Longitude=X)
  Sys.sleep(5)
  
}

title: Load data
text:
Load census data
To estimate catchment populations for transplant centers, we retrieve tract- and county-level population data from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files. Because these data are large and slow to download, we implement a caching strategy to avoid repeated API calls during iterative renders.

Overview
For each year in year_list, this code:

Retrieves tract-level total population
Retrieves county-level total population
Caches results locally as .rds files

This structure ensures reproducibility while dramatically improving performance during Quarto re-rendering.


Tract-Level Population Data
We obtain tract-level total population using ACS variable:

B01003_001 — Total population

If a cached file already exists (cache/us_tracts_population_YEAR.rds), it is loaded directly. Otherwise:

Data are downloaded using get_acs()
Geometry is included (geometry = TRUE) for spatial joins
County FIPS codes are derived from the first five digits of the tract GEOID
Identifier fields are converted to numeric for efficient joins
Only necessary variables are retained
The cleaned dataset is saved locally for future use


Why include geometry?
Including tract geometry allows direct spatial intersection with:

50-mile buffers
60-minute isochrones
United catchment areas

This avoids needing a second shapefile join later.



County-Level Population Data
County-level total population is retrieved using the same ACS variable (B01003_001), with geometry retained.
County data are used for:

County-level HIV prevalence overlays
Aggregated catchment summaries
Validation checks against tract-level totals

As with tract data, results are cached locally to prevent redundant API calls.


Age and Sex Variable Labels (B01001)
The ACS table B01001 contains detailed age- and sex-specific population counts. Rather than downloading these counts directly in this step, we load the variable metadata using:


Click to show/hide R Code
# Load census data
us_tracts_population<-list()
us_counties_population<-list()
vars<-list()

for (year_loop in year_list){
  
  
  tracts_path<-paste0("cache/us_tracts_population_",year_loop,".rds")
  counties_path<-paste0("cache/us_counties_population_",year_loop,".rds")
  
  #Pull US Census tract populations if cache file doesn't already exist
  
  if (file.exists(tracts_path)) {
    us_tracts_population[[year_loop]] <- readRDS(tracts_path)
  } else {
    
    us_tracts_population[[year_loop]]<-get_acs(
      geography = "tract",
      variables = "B01003_001",
      year = as.numeric(year_loop),
      survey = "acs5",
      geometry = TRUE,
      state = continental_fips
    )%>%
      mutate(county_fips = substr(GEOID, 1, 5))%>%
      mutate(GEOID=as.numeric(GEOID))%>%
      mutate(county_fips=as.numeric(county_fips))%>%
      select(-variable, -moe)%>%
      rename(tract_population=estimate)
    
    saveRDS(us_tracts_population[[year_loop]], 
            tracts_path)
    
  }
  
  #Pull US Census counties populations if cache file doesn't already exist
  
  if (file.exists(counties_path)) {
    us_counties_population[[year_loop]] <- readRDS(counties_path)
  } else {
    
    us_counties_population[[year_loop]]<-get_acs(
      geography = "county",
      variables = "B01003_001",
      year = as.numeric(year_loop),
      survey = "acs5",
      geometry = TRUE,
      state = continental_fips
    )%>%
      mutate(GEOID=as.numeric(GEOID))%>%
      select(-variable, -moe)%>%
      rename(county_population=estimate)
    
    saveRDS(us_counties_population[[year_loop]], 
            counties_path)
    
    
  }
  
  # Load tract variable labels for age/sex values B01001 from the ACS 5-year 2017 dataset
  vars[[year_loop]] <- load_variables(year_loop, "acs5", cache = TRUE) %>%
    filter(str_detect(name, "B01001_"))%>%
    mutate(label = str_replace_all(label, "Estimate!!Total!!", ""))%>%
    mutate(label = str_replace_all(label, "!!", "_"))%>%
    mutate(label = str_replace_all(label, " ", "_"))
  
}

title: Join tracts to buffers
text:
This section identifies which census tracts fall within transplant center catchment areas.
Earlier steps created:
Here, we determine which tracts intersect each center’s catchment area using spatial joins.

title: Join tracts to buffers
section: Linking Census Tracts to Transplant Center Catchment Areas
text:
Linking Census Tracts to Transplant Center Catchment Areas
This code performs spatial intersection joins between:

Census tract–level data (Merged_tracts)
Transplant center buffer polygons

The goal is to determine which tracts are geographically reachable from transplant centers under each scenario.

title: Join tracts to buffers
text:
Objects Created
Three nested list objects are generated:

tracts_in_buffers_active
tracts_in_buffers_HIV
tracts_in_buffers_HOPE

Each is indexed by:

Organ

Distance

Year

title: Join tracts to buffers
text:
What the Spatial Join Does
For each:

Organ

Distance

Year

The script performs:
st_join(…, join = st_intersects)
This means:

A census tract is included if its geometry intersects the transplant center buffer polygon.

In practical terms:

If any part of a tract lies within a center’s catchment area,
That tract is considered geographically accessible to that center.

title: Join tracts to buffers
text:
Important Note on Duplication
Because this join is performed against individual center buffers, a tract can appear multiple times if:

It falls within the catchment area of more than one transplant center.

This duplication is intentional at this stage because:

It preserves center-level relationships.
It allows downstream analyses of overlap and multi-center accessibility.

Later steps that use united buffers eliminate this duplication when calculating total population coverage.

title: Join tracts to buffers
text:
Why This Step Matters
This spatial join enables calculation of:

Number of people living with HIV within reach of transplant centers
Differences in geographic access between:

Active centers
HIV R+ centers
HOPE centers

Changes over time (e.g., 2017 vs 2022)

By linking tract-level population data to center catchment areas, the analysis translates geography into measurable access.



Click to show/hide R Code
#ST join to individual tracts and transplant centers


tracts_in_buffers_active<-list()
tracts_in_buffers_HIV<-list()
tracts_in_buffers_HOPE<-list()




for (organ_loop in organ_list){
  for (distance_loop in distance_list){
    for (year_loop in year_list){

      message(paste("Currently on:", organ_loop, "", distance_loop, "for year:", year_loop))
      message("Calculating tracts for active...")
      
      #This leads to duplication of tracts if they fall in more than one transplant center's catchment area)      
      tracts_in_buffers_active[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]] <- 
        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]], 
                Transplant_centers_active_buffer[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], 
                join = st_intersects)
      
      
      message("Calculating tracts for HIV...")
      
      tracts_in_buffers_HIV[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]] <- 
        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]], 
                Transplant_centers_HIV_buffer[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], 
                join = st_intersects)
      
      message("Calculating tracts for HOPE...")
      
      tracts_in_buffers_HOPE[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]] <- 
        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]], 
                Transplant_centers_HOPE_buffer[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], 
                join = st_intersects)

      
            
    }
  }
}

text:
Figures
Figures are grouped into three sections.


Compare PLWH and non-HIV
These figures compare geographic access between PLWH and individuals without HIV within each catchment definition.
Each panel corresponds to a distance-based definition:

50 miles

60 minutes

100 miles

200 miles

These figures highlight disparities in access by HIV status.


































Compare PLWH Between Years
These figures evaluate changes in geographic access among PLWH between 2017 and 2022.
For each catchment definition, results are shown for:

Active centers

HIV R+ centers

This section highlights temporal changes in transplant center availability.






























































Beeswarm Plots
Beeswarm plots display the distribution of catchment-level population proportions across centers.
Each point represents a transplant center, with the distribution shown for each distance definition.
These plots illustrate variability in geographic access across centers rather than only aggregate proportions.
Project documentsArchitecture Code

Overview
This project estimates what share of people living with HIV (PLWH) in the continental United States live within reach of an adult solid-organ transplant center, and compares that with people without HIV. It covers five organs (kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas), two index years (2017, 2022), and four reach definitions: 50, 100 and 200 mile straight-line buffers, and a 60-minute driving isochrone. Centers are grouped three ways: all active adult centers, centers that transplanted a recipient with HIV (HIV R+), and centers that used an HIV-positive donor (HOPE D+).
The project has two layers:

A sequential R pipeline (R/main.R) that builds every object as a named list in the global environment and writes tables, figures and cached objects to disk. Its last steps copy the tables and figures the website shows into site-outputs/, which is committed.
A Quarto website (_quarto.yml) that documents each script and shows results by reading site-outputs/. A GitHub Actions workflow renders it and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. The website never runs the analysis and needs no restricted data.

Execution order
R/main.R sources the scripts in this order. Each script reads objects the earlier ones left in the global environment.

R/setup.R, R/functions.R
R/load_data.R
R/classify_centers.R
R/county_geographic_calculations.R
R/geographical_computations_for_centers.R
R/set_isochrones.R
R/unite_buffers.R
R/join_tracts_to_buffers.R
R/join_tracts_to_united_buffers.R
R/calculate_aggregated_results.R

Components

Setup and helpers
Location: R/setup.R, R/functions.R
Purpose: Loads the analysis packages and defines the analysis grid and shared helper functions.
Key definitions (R/setup.R): - organ_list, year_list, distance_list — drive every loop in the pipeline - continental_fips — states included in Census pulls - timezones, reference_date — used to time isochrones at 7 AM local on the first Monday in March of each index year
Key functions (R/functions.R): - set_60_min_isochrone_at_7AM() — groups centers by time zone and calls mapboxapi::mb_isochrone() with a 7 AM local departure - convert_resultsdf_to_table() — builds the gt results tables - make_paired_plot(), plot_center_HIV_catchment() — plotting helpers, described under Figures


Data loading
Location: R/load_data.R
Inputs: - SRTR transplant files via load_srtr_file(), plus deceased-donor HIV fields (DON_ANTI_HIV, DON_HIV_NAT) - HRSA transplant centers via sRtr::get_hrsa_transplant_centers(), filtered by organ from Service_Lst, excluding Puerto Rico and Hawaii - ACS 5-year total population (B01003_001) for tracts and counties - CDC AtlasPlus county HIV prevalence via CDCAtlas::get_atlas() - State outlines via tigris::states()
Outputs: tx, donor_deceased, Transplant_centers_all, us_tracts_population, us_counties_population, AtlasPlusTableData_county_totals, vars, states_sf
Caching: ACS pulls are cached to cache/us_tracts_population_<year>.rds and cache/us_counties_population_<year>.rds. HRSA and AtlasPlus are fetched live on every run.


Center classification
Location: R/classify_centers.R
Purpose: Defines the three center groups for each organ and year.

Active: at least one adult (age ≥ 216 months) transplant in the index calendar year.
HIV R+ volume: adult recipients with HIV over the five years ending in the index year, restricted to active centers.
HOPE D+ volume: adult recipients with HIV over the same window whose donor was HIV-positive by NAT or antibody.

Outputs: Active_tx_centers, HIV_center_volumes, HOPE_center_volumes, State_level_transplant_volumes, Transplant_centers_active


County-to-tract allocation
Location: R/county_geographic_calculations.R
Purpose: Projects center points to EPSG:5070 (CONUS Albers, meters), builds the HIV and HOPE center subsets, and estimates tract-level HIV counts.

AtlasPlus county cases are joined to ACS counties by numeric GEOID.
Each tract receives a share of its county’s cases in proportion to its population (tract_cases). tract_noncases is tract population minus tract_cases.
These tract counts are estimates that assume HIV prevalence is uniform within a county.

Outputs: Transplant_centers_all_sf, Transplant_centers_active_SF, Transplant_centers_HIV_sf, Transplant_centers_HOPE_sf, Merged_Counties, Merged_tracts


Reach geometry
Location: R/geographical_computations_for_centers.R, R/set_isochrones.R, R/unite_buffers.R

Mile buffers: st_buffer() in meters on EPSG:5070 (50 mi = 80,467.2 m; 100 mi = 160,934.4 m; 200 mi = 321,868 m).
Isochrones: 60 minutes, driving-traffic profile, departing 7 AM local time on the reference date. Each center’s time zone comes from lutz::tz_lookup(). Results are cached per organ, year and center group in cache/Transplant_center(s)_*_60min_buffer_*.RDS. The all-centers isochrone uses the 2017 reference date.
Mile buffers and isochrones are stored in the same nested lists (Transplant_centers_*_buffer[[organ]][[distance]][[year]]), so every downstream step treats the four reach definitions the same way.
Union: each set of buffers is dissolved into a single catchment polygon (catchment_area = "All Centers").

Outputs: Transplant_center*_buffer (per center) and Transplant_center*_buffer_united (dissolved), nested by organ, distance and year


Tract joins and aggregation
Location: R/join_tracts_to_united_buffers.R, R/calculate_aggregated_results.R, R/join_tracts_to_buffers.R
These are two independent branches from the buffers, not a sequence.

United branch (results tables): tracts are joined to the dissolved catchment with st_intersects, so each tract counts once. Aggregation sums tract_cases (active, HIV R+ and HOPE D+ groups) and tract_noncases (active group only) for intersecting tracts, divided by the national tract totals. Outputs: tracts_in_buffers_*_united, Results_HIV_df, Results_nonHIV_df.
Per-center branch (beeswarm figures): tracts are joined to each center’s own buffer. A tract inside several catchments appears once per center, which is intended here because the figure shows each center’s own catchment. Outputs: tracts_in_buffers_active, tracts_in_buffers_HIV, tracts_in_buffers_HOPE. Only tracts_in_buffers_active is used downstream.

title: Overview
text:
Solid organ transplantation has transformed survival for patients with end-stage organ disease. For people living with HIV (PLWH), access to transplantation has historically been limited by medical uncertainty, regulatory restrictions, and stigma. Over the past two decades, however, advances in antiretroviral therapy (ART) and transplant immunology have substantially changed the clinical landscape.
This project integrates HIV epidemiologic data with SRTR transplant center data to examine geographic access to HIV-experienced transplant programs across the United States.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
This project evaluates geographic access to solid organ transplant centers for people living with HIV in the United States. County-level HIV prevalence data from the CDC NCHHSTP AtlasPlus system were integrated with national transplant center location data. Transplant centers were classified by activity status and HIV program participation (including HOPE Act programs).
Geographic accessibility was estimated using drive-time isochrones generated at standardized morning departure times. Isochrones were unioned across centers and spatially joined to county and tract-level population data to estimate the number and proportion of people living with HIV within defined travel-time thresholds.
All data processing and spatial analyses were conducted in R using reproducible workflows built on {sf}, {tigris}, and custom functions documented throughout this site. No spatial smoothing or statistical modeling was applied unless explicitly stated.
Braces identify R packages throughout this site.

title: Join tracts to united buffers
text:
This section performs spatial joins between census tracts and the united (merged) transplant center buffers.
Unlike the earlier version—where tracts were joined to individual center buffers—this approach joins tracts to a single merged catchment polygon for each organ, distance, and year.
This prevents duplication and ensures accurate population totals.






RcodeSource code

text:
This section performs spatial joins between census tracts and the united (merged) transplant center buffers.
Unlike the earlier version—where tracts were joined to individual center buffers—this approach joins tracts to a single merged catchment polygon for each organ, distance, and year.
This prevents duplication and ensures accurate population totals.

title: Join tracts to united buffers
text:
Why Use United Buffers?
When joining tracts to individual center buffers:

A tract can intersect multiple centers
That tract would appear multiple times
Population totals would be inflated unless deduplicated later

By first uniting buffers using st_union() and then joining:

Each tract appears at most once
Population counts reflect total geographic coverage
Overlapping service areas are handled correctly

This is essential for valid total-access calculations.

title: Join tracts to united buffers
text:
Objects Created
Three nested list objects are generated:

tracts_in_buffers_active_united
tracts_in_buffers_HIV_united
tracts_in_buffers_HOPE_united

Each object is indexed by:

Organ

Distance

title: Join tracts to united buffers
text:
What the Spatial Join Does
For each:

Organ

Distance

Year

The script performs:
st_join(..., join = st_intersects)
This means:

A census tract is included if it intersects the combined catchment area of that transplant center group.

Because the buffer has already been united:

Each tract can match only once per category
No duplication occurs due to overlapping center service areas

title: Join tracts to united buffers
text:
Why This Step Matters
This unified join enables accurate calculation of:

Total population within reach of transplant services

Total number of people living with HIV within those catchment areas

Changes in geographic access across years

Comparisons between Active, HIV R+, and HOPE centers

By eliminating overlap-driven duplication, this approach ensures that access estimates reflect true geographic coverage, not inflated counts.

tracts_in_buffers_active_united<-list()
tracts_in_buffers_HIV_united<-list()
tracts_in_buffers_HOPE_united<-list()

for (organ_loop in organ_list){
  for (distance_loop in distance_list){
    for (year_loop in year_list){
      
      message(paste("Currently on:", organ_loop, "", distance_loop, "for year:", year_loop))
      message("Calculating tracts for active...")
      
      #ST join to individual tracts and the united transplant center geography to avoid duplication
      tracts_in_buffers_active_united[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]] <- 
        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]], 
                Transplant_centers_active_buffer_united[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], 
                join = st_intersects)
      
      message("Calculating tracts for HIV...")

        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]],

                join = st_intersects)
      
      message("Calculating tracts for HOPE...")
      tracts_in_buffers_HOPE_united[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]] <- 
        st_join(Merged_tracts[[year_loop]], 
                Transplant_centers_HOPE_buffer_united[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], 
                join = st_intersects)

section: Initialize Result Containers and Baseline Totals
text:
Initialize Result Containers and Baseline Totals
This first section prepares the data structures that will store aggregated coverage results and calculates the population baselines used as denominators.

Step 1: Create Empty Results Tables
For each organ, two empty result tables are initialized:

Results_HIV_df — for people living with HIV (PLWH)
Results_nonHIV_df — for people without HIV

Each table is structured to store:

Characteristic — the center category and distance (e.g., active 60min)
Numerator — population within the catchment area
Denominator — total population nationwide (for that year)
Percentage — share of the total population within reach
Year — analysis year

These tables will be filled in later sections of the script.



Step 2: Calculate Total Population Denominators
Before computing coverage percentages, we calculate the total estimated population counts across all census tracts.
For each year:

The total number of estimated HIV cases (tract_cases) is summed across all tracts.
The total estimated HIV-negative population (tract_noncases) is summed across all tracts.
Geometry is dropped before summarizing to improve computational efficiency.

These totals are stored in:

Tract_total_HIV_cases[[year]]
Tract_total_nonHIV_cases[[year]]

These values serve as the denominators for all subsequent percentage calculations.


Click to show/hide R Code
Results_HIV_df<-list()
Results_nonHIV_df<-list()
Tract_total_HIV_cases<-list()
Tract_total_nonHIV_cases<-list()
                      
for (organ_loop in organ_list)
  
{
  
  #Initialize data frames
  Results_HIV_df[[organ_loop]] <- tibble(
    Characteristic = character(),
    Numerator = numeric(),
    Denominator = numeric(),
    Percentage = numeric(),
    Year= numeric()
  )
  
  Results_nonHIV_df[[organ_loop]] <- tibble(
    Characteristic = character(),
    Numerator = numeric(),
    Denominator = numeric(),
    Percentage = numeric(),
    Year= numeric()
  )
}
  
  for (year_loop in year_list)
  {
  
  #Calculate the total number of HIV cases assigned to a tract
  Tract_total_HIV_cases[[year_loop]]<-Merged_tracts[[year_loop]]%>%
    st_drop_geometry()%>%
    summarize(total_cases=sum(tract_cases, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
    pull(total_cases)%>%
    first()
  
  #Calculate the total number of nonHIV cases (i.e. people without HIV) assigned to a tract
  Tract_total_nonHIV_cases[[year_loop]]<-Merged_tracts[[year_loop]]%>%
    st_drop_geometry()%>%
    summarize(total_cases=sum(tract_noncases, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
    pull(total_cases)%>%
    first()
}

section: Aggregate Coverage Results for People Living with HIV (PLWH)
text:
Aggregate Coverage Results for People Living with HIV (PLWH)
This section calculates the proportion of people living with HIV who reside within transplant center catchment areas.
For each:

Organ

Distance (e.g., 50 miles, 60 minutes)

Year

Center category (active, HIV, HOPE)

the script computes:

The numerator: total estimated HIV cases (tract_cases) located within the united catchment area

The denominator: total estimated HIV cases across all census tracts for that year

The percentage: share of PLWH within geographic reach


How It Works
For each combination of organ, distance, year, and center type:

The appropriate united tract-buffer object is dynamically selected.
Geometry is dropped to improve efficiency.
Tract-level HIV cases are summed within the catchment area.
That sum is divided by the national total for the year.
A new row is appended to Results_HIV_df[[organ]].

The resulting table quantifies geographic access to transplant services for people living with HIV and enables comparison:

Across organs

Across distances

Across center categories

Across time (e.g., 2017 vs 2022)



Click to show/hide R Code
#Calculate table for PLWH


for (organ_loop in organ_list)
{
  for (distance_loop in distance_list){
    for (year_loop in year_list){
      for (type in c("active", "HIV", "HOPE")) {
        
        name_of_df<-paste0("tracts_in_buffers_", type, "_united")
        print(name_of_df)
        
        temp_Num<-get(name_of_df)[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]]%>%
          st_drop_geometry()%>%
          group_by(catchment_area)%>%
          summarize(total_cases=sum(tract_cases, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
          pull(total_cases)%>%
          first()
        
        temp_Denom<-Tract_total_HIV_cases[[year_loop]]
        
        
        Results_HIV_df[[organ_loop]]<-Results_HIV_df[[organ_loop]]%>%
          add_row(
            Characteristic = paste(type, distance_loop),
            Numerator = round(temp_Num, 0),
            Denominator = temp_Denom,
            Percentage = round(100*temp_Num/temp_Denom,1),
            Year= as.numeric(year_loop)
          ) 
        
      }
    }
  }
}

title: Calculate aggregated results
section: Aggregate Coverage Results for People Without HIV
text:
Aggregate Coverage Results for People Without HIV
This final section calculates geographic coverage for the population without HIV.
The structure mirrors the PLWH calculation but uses:

tract_noncases instead of tract_cases
Tract_total_nonHIV_cases as the denominator


What Is Being Calculated?
For each:

Organ

Distance

Year

the script computes:

The numerator: total estimated non-HIV population within the united active-center catchment area

The denominator: total estimated non-HIV population across all census tracts for that year

The percentage: share of the non-HIV population within geographic reach



Why Only Active Centers?
In this implementation, non-HIV coverage is calculated for active transplant centers only.
This provides a general population access benchmark that can be compared against:

Coverage for people living with HIV

Coverage within HIV-performing or HOPE-performing center categories



How It Works
For each organ, distance, and year:

The united active-center tract object is selected.
Geometry is dropped for efficient aggregation.
tract_noncases is summed within the catchment area.
The total is divided by the national non-HIV population estimate for that year.
A new row is appended to Results_nonHIV_df[[organ]].


These results allow comparison between:

Geographic access for people living with HIV

Geographic access for the general population

Changes over time

Differences across organ types and service-area definitions

Together, the PLWH and non-HIV tables provide the quantitative foundation for the manuscript’s access comparisons.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Calculate tract-level results for people without HIV
for (organ_loop in organ_list)
{
  for (distance_loop in distance_list){
    for (year_loop in year_list){
      for (type in c("active")) {
        
        name_of_df<-paste0("tracts_in_buffers_", type, "_united")
        print(name_of_df)
        
        temp_Num<-get(name_of_df)[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]]%>%
          st_drop_geometry()%>%
          group_by(catchment_area)%>%
          summarize(total_noncases=sum(tract_noncases, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
          pull(total_noncases)%>%
          first()
        
        temp_Denom<-Tract_total_nonHIV_cases[[year_loop]]
        
        Results_nonHIV_df[[organ_loop]]<-Results_nonHIV_df[[organ_loop]]%>%
          add_row(
            Characteristic = paste(type, distance_loop),
            Numerator = round(temp_Num, 0),
            Denominator = temp_Denom,
            Percentage = round(100*temp_Num/temp_Denom,1),
            Year= as.numeric(year_loop))
        
        
        
      }
    }
  }
  
}

title: Figures
text:
Create Dot-Density Spatial Objects
This section prepares spatial objects used to visualize the geographic distribution of HIV cases.
Rather than shading counties by case counts (a choropleth), this approach uses a dot-density map, where:

Each dot represents a fixed number of HIV cases

Dots are distributed within county boundaries

Higher-density areas visually reflect greater case burden



Why Use Dot-Density Maps?
Dot-density maps have several advantages:

They avoid misleading visual effects caused by large but sparsely populated counties

They better reflect population concentration rather than land area

They provide a more intuitive visual representation of case burden

In this implementation:

Each dot represents 100 HIV cases
Dots are generated from the county-level county_cases variable




Objects Created
Two spatial lists are generated:

county_dots — raw dot-density geometries
county_dots_transformed — projected versions for mapping

For each year:

as_dot_density() converts county-level HIV case counts into dot geometries.
The resulting points are transformed to EPSG:5070 (NAD83 / Conus Albers) for consistency with other spatial layers.




Map Projection Standardization
The U.S. state boundary map (states_sf) is also transformed to EPSG:5070.
Using a consistent projected coordinate reference system ensures:

Accurate spatial alignment
Correct scaling
Consistent appearance across figures
Proper overlay with transplant center buffers and tract-level data


These spatial objects are later layered into manuscript figures to visualize:

Geographic HIV burden
Overlay with transplant center service areas
Changes across years

# Create dot plot sf data frames

county_dots<-list()
county_dots_transformed<-list()


for (year_loop in year_list)
  
{
  
  county_dots[[year_loop]]<-as_dot_density(Merged_Counties[[year_loop]], 
                                           "county_cases", 
                                           values_per_dot =100)
  
  county_dots_transformed[[year_loop]]<-county_dots[[year_loop]]%>%
    st_transform(5070)
  
}

#Transform us state map
states_sf_transformed<-states_sf%>%
  st_transform(5070)

Maps of Active and HIV-Performing Transplant Centers
This section generates manuscript-ready maps that overlay transplant center catchment areas on top of the national HIV dot-density map.

Organ

Year

two types of figures are created:

Active transplant center maps

Map Layers
Each figure includes three spatial layers:

Dot-density HIV layer

Derived from county-level HIV case counts

Each dot represents 100 HIV cases

Provides visual context for geographic burden

Transplant center catchment areas

Either active-center buffers or HIV R+ buffers

Displayed as red outlines

Represent geographic access zones

U.S. state boundaries

Provide geographic reference

Drawn without fill for clarity


All layers use the same projected coordinate system (EPSG:5070) to ensure proper alignment.



Active Center Maps
These maps show:

All active transplant centers for a given organ
Their associated catchment areas
Overlayed on national HIV case distribution

The title specifies:

Organ type

Year

Each figure is saved as an .svg file in the corresponding organ-specific folder.



HIV R+ Center Maps
These maps focus specifically on:

Centers that performed HIV R+ transplants

Their catchment areas

Overlayed on HIV case distribution

The title reflects the analysis year (e.g., 2013–2017 window where applicable).
These figures visually illustrate:

How geographic access for PLWH changes over time

Differences between general active centers and HIV-performing centers

Regions with high HIV burden but limited transplant access




Why These Maps Matter
These figures translate the analytic results into intuitive geographic visualizations that allow readers to:

See where HIV burden is concentrated

Identify regions lacking nearby transplant access

Compare service-area expansion or contraction across years

Assess disparities between general and HIV-specific transplant availability

The resulting .svg files are publication-quality and scalable for manuscript submission.

        theme_minimal() +

             subtitle = "(1 dot = 100 HIV cases)")+
        geom_sf(data=Transplant_centers_active_buffer[[organ_loop]][[distance_loop]][[year_loop]], color="red", fill=NA)+
        geom_sf(data=states_sf_transformed, fill=NA)

text:
Paired Plots for PLWH Comparing Years
This section generates side-by-side comparison plots to visualize changes in geographic access between 2017 and 2022.
Rather than showing maps, these figures present paired summary plots that directly compare:

Coverage in 2017

Coverage in 2022

for each organ, distance definition, and center category.


What These Plots Show
For each:

Organ

Distance (e.g., 50 miles, 60 minutes)

the script produces paired plots for:

Active transplant centers

Active centers (with optional comparison of PLWH vs non-HIV population)

HIV R+ centers

HOPE (HIV D+/R+) centers

Each plot compares the percentage of the population within geographic reach across the two years.



How the Plots Are Created
All plots are generated using a reusable helper function:
make_paired_plot()
This function:

Extracts aggregated results

Aligns year-specific values

Formats titles and labels

Produces consistent visual styling

The distance_label variable converts internal codes (e.g., 50mile, 60min) into reader-friendly labels such as:

“50 miles”
“60 mins”




Comparing PLWH and Non-HIV Populations
For active centers, a second version of the paired plot is generated with:
include_nonHIV = TRUE
This version overlays:

Coverage for people living with HIV

Coverage for the non-HIV population

This allows visual assessment of whether geographic access differs between populations.



Output Format
Each plot is saved in two formats:

.svg — publication-quality vector graphics

.png — presentation-friendly raster format

Images are saved at:

Width: 12 inches

Height: 6 inches

White background

High-resolution rendering via {ragg}




Why These Figures Matter
These paired plots provide a clear visual summary of:

Expansion or contraction of transplant access over time

Differences between center categories

Potential disparities in geographic coverage

Organ-specific variation in access

They translate tabular percentage changes into intuitive, publication-ready visuals suitable for the manuscript.

Copying Figures to the Website Folder
The website does not read figures/, which is not committed. This last step copies the figures the website shows into site-outputs/figures/, which is committed and published by the site’s build.

What This Step Does

Builds the list of figures the results pages and the methods page show: for each organ and reach definition, the paired plot comparing PLWH with people without HIV, the three center-group plots (active, HIV R+, HOPE D+) and the beeswarm plot, plus the access model diagram. That is 101 files.
Stops with an error naming any figure on the list that was not created, so a missing plot cannot quietly drop off the site.
Copies the listed files, and only those, into site-outputs/figures/, keeping each organ’s folder.

Because only named files are copied, older or experimental files left in figures/ never reach the site.


Before Committing
site-outputs/ is public once committed. The copy step does not decide what is published: after a run, review the changed files for disclosure under the SRTR data use agreement before committing them. The center-group and beeswarm plots draw on SRTR-derived center classifications.

title: Clinical background
text:
Solid organ transplantation has transformed survival for patients with end-stage organ disease. For people living with HIV (PLWH), access to transplantation has historically been limited by medical uncertainty, regulatory restrictions, and stigma. Over the past two decades, durable viral suppression with modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) and accumulated transplant experience have reshaped the clinical landscape.
This project integrates HIV epidemiologic data with SRTR transplant center information to examine geographic access to HIV-experienced transplant programs across the United States.
